The foundational framework emerges from a deterministic attractor landscape where each stable configuration represents a genetic type. The polygonal metaphor implies a discrete set of attractors, each with a basin of attraction. Equilibrium reversion captures the tendency to return to prior stable states under disturbance, modeled as a restoring force. Variability bounds reflect the constraint that fluctuations remain within permissible limits, preserving breed identity. Reversion tendency describes the mechanism by which deviations from a sub-type revert to an earlier form, suggesting a hierarchical structure of trait inheritance. Stable sports indicate that rare mutations can persist across generations, implying a non-linear feedback loop between novelty and stability. These operators define a dualistic system: one of bounded fluctuation and another of emergent persistence. Failure modes arise when perturbations exceed basin boundaries or when genetic drift destabilizes established attractors. The interplay between these components yields a robust model of evolutionary stability.
